text: DELETE isn't the only way to empty a table. In this lesson you'll compare it to TRUNCATE TABLE and see where the two genuinely differ.

TRUNCATE TABLE removes every row from a table in one step. DELETE FROM with no WHERE produces the same end result -- zero rows -- but the two work differently under the hood, with real side effects that matter.
TRUNCATE TABLE has no WHERE clause option at all -- it is strictly all or nothing on the whole table. If you need to remove only some rows, DELETE FROM with a WHERE clause is the only choice.

Here's the difference that trips people up most. Delete every row, then insert a new one, and the IDENTITY counter continues from where it left off -- it does not reset, even though the table is empty.
Truncate the same table instead, then insert a new row, and ProductID restarts at 1. TRUNCATE TABLE resets the identity seed back to its starting value, which DELETE never does.
Next, you'll learn the OUTPUT clause, which lets an INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE statement return exactly which rows it touched.
